paras: The killing of Robert Charles and the New Orleans race riot was a series of white mob attacks on Black residents of New Orleans in late July 1900, set off when Charles, a Black man, was accused of shooting three policemen, and ended by his death in a burning house on Friday, July 27. Wire reports counted twelve dead and twenty-eight wounded, mixing mob victims with the officers and citizens Charles was accused of shooting. A grand jury indicted both white mob members and Black people accused of aiding Charles, and Black weeklies treated the riot as a national question.

According to the wire account, police called to two "suspicious" Black men clashed with them; Officer Mora was shot and Charles escaped, wounded. When Capt. John T. Day led a party to his lodging, Charles was accused of killing Day and Patrolman Lamb with a Winchester. The Richmond Planet said instead that the officer had tried to arrest Charles "without a warrant" when he had committed no crime. White reports called him a "desperado" and, citing police, a burglar and ex-convict; the wire also blamed white workers' resentment of Black levee labor for police reluctance to act.

A dispatch dated July 26 described a "mob of white boys" that hunted Black people overnight, killing three unidentified men, beating Baptist Filo, aged 75, and Esther Fields, and dragging the porter Alex. Ruffin from a streetcar, while police were "powerless." August Thomas was killed at Custom House and Villere streets and Lewis Taylor died after being shot and clubbed at the French Market. Early on July 27 a mob broke into a Rousseau Street house and shot an elderly Black woman named Mabry.

That Friday police went to a house on Saratoga Street, where Charles was accused of killing Sgt. Gabriel Porteous, Andy Van Kurem and a youth, Alfred J. Bloomfield, and wounding others, as a crowd put at 20,000 gathered. Someone set the building afire, and as Charles came out a militiaman, Adolph Anderson, was credited with shooting him. Armed men fired into the body, and police and mob "emptied their revolvers into it" in the street until police carried it off amid calls to burn it. A Black man found in the house was shot dead in police hands, another was killed on Gallatin Street, and that night a mob burned the Thomy Lafon school for Black children.

Order returned with 1,500 special police and the militia on the streets, and colored ministers adopted resolutions condemning Charles and thanking the mayor. The grand jury indicted five white men as mob leaders and six Black men as Charles's accessories, then five more white men, including S. F. McCowan as organizer of the July 25 mob, and the militiaman William Burke for killing the man from the house. On September 12 objection was made that no Black men sat on that grand jury; no report of a trial appears in the coverage.

South Carolina weeklies ran the wire under headlines such as "NEGRO MURDERERS" while reporting that police were "sympathetic with the mobs." Northern white papers condemned the mob, the Daily Kennebec Journal calling the school burning "the crowning infamy." Black weeklies reprinted the wire copy, the Savannah Tribune even calling Charles "a hater of the white race," but their editorials differed. The Richmond Planet called it "butchery" and the Indianapolis Freeman said Black people were "hunted as rabbits." The Plaindealer, the Seattle Republican and the Cleveland Gazette praised Charles for selling his life dearly. By late August Black editors linked New Orleans to violence in New York and Chicago.

Counts differed: twelve dead in wire reports, eight white men killed by Charles in the Savannah copy, eleven in the Seattle Republican. The man killed after the siege was called Charles's "companion" in one report and a prisoner shot by a mob member in another, while the grand jury named a militiaman.

reader.title: Killing of Robert Charles and the New Orleans race riot
bases: White mobs hunted, beat and shot Black residents across New Orleans over several days and burned a Black school, set off by Robert Charles's alleged shooting of police and ending with his death in a police, militia and crowd siege (A1, A4, A2, A12).

Separate dispatches and later reports agree on the police shootings, the mob attacks, the Saratoga Street siege and Charles's death, and grand jury indictments followed (A1, A3, A4, A14, A20, A23, A26).

accounts.label: Wire report (police version)
accounts.gist: Two 'suspicious' Black men resisted police; Charles shot Mora, killed Day and Lamb, then killed and wounded more in the siege until he was burned out and shot.

accounts.label: Richmond Planet
accounts.gist: Charles shot an officer who tried to arrest him without a warrant when he had committed no crime; police then encouraged a mob that shot down law-abiding Black people.

accounts.label: Overnight mob dispatch
accounts.gist: A leaderless mob of white boys hunted Black people through the night of July 25-26, killing three and wounding others, while police were powerless.

accounts.label: Grand jury
accounts.gist: Indicted white mob leaders and a militiaman for killings, and the Black occupants of the Jackson house as accessories to Charles.

accounts.label: Colored ministers of New Orleans
accounts.gist: Condemned Charles's career and thanked the mayor and citizen police for protecting Black residents.

framing.detail: Southern wire copy headlined 'NEGRO MURDERERS' and 'desperado' while reporting mob outrages on Black people and police sympathy with the mobs.
Northern editorials called the Lafon school burning the 'crowning infamy' and said the South did not confine its violence to the guilty.
Colored Citizen, Indianapolis Recorder, Richmond Planet and Savannah Tribune ran the wire account, including its 'desperado' language.
Editorials called it 'butchery', said Black people were 'hunted as rabbits', blamed the police and the Democratic party, and some praised Charles for selling his life dearly.

record_check.record: Robert Charles, Bloomfield, Anna Mabry, Captain Day, Patrol Lamb, Lewis Taylor, August Thomas, ... Porteous, Lally, Lamb, Van Kurem, Sly Jackson
record_check.dossier: Mixes the Black victims of the mobs and siege (Charles, Thomas, Taylor, Mabry, the unknown Jackson-house and Gallatin Street men, Filo) with the white officers and citizens Charles was accused of shooting (Day, Lamb, Porteous, Lally, Van Kurem, Bloomfield), who were not targets of the attack; Lally appears three times; 'Sly Jackson' does not appear in these texts.
At least six named or distinct Black dead, plus three unidentified men killed July 25-26 who may overlap.
Six white dead named (Day, Lamb, Porteous, Lally, Van Kurem, Bloomfield), all attributed to Charles, not to the mobs; one wire says eight.
Charles was at large and besieged when killed; only the unknown Jackson-house man was killed in police hands.
White mobs; police, special police, militia and citizens at the siege; named and indicted: Flanagan, Foley, Carl, McCowan, Wagner, Burke.
Date of the siege and Charles's death and the Mabry and Lafon school attacks; the riot began July 23-25.

record_check.record: Charles ... smoked out ... shot to pieces. An unknown Black man was also killed ...
record_check.dossier: Omits the multi-day mob attacks, the school burning and the indictments of white mob leaders and of Black occupants of the house.

info: Riot ran from the night Day and Lamb were shot (Monday or Tuesday, July 23 or 24) to the night of Friday, July 27; Charles killed the afternoon of Friday, July 27.
New Orleans; Charles killed in a house on Saratoga Street (near Clio); mob attacks in the French Market, Custom House and Villere streets, Rousseau Street, Gallatin Street and elsewhere.

Robert Charles; an unidentified Black man killed in police hands after the siege (buried as Burke Jackson); an unknown Black man killed on Gallatin Street; August Thomas; Lewis (Louis) Taylor; Anna (or Hannah) Mabry; three unidentified Black men killed the night of July 25-26; injured include Baptist Filo, Alex. Ruffin, T. P. Anders, Esther Fields, George Morris, Dan White.

Charles was accused of shooting Officer Mora and killing Capt. John T. Day and Patrolman Lamb, then in the siege of killing Sgt. Gabriel Porteous, Andy Van Kurem and Alfred J. Bloomfield and wounding others.

White mobs (described as boys and 'hoodlums'); in the siege, police, special police, militia and armed citizens; named accused: George Flanagan, Mike Foley, E. F. Carl, S. F. McCowan, Joseph Wagner, militiaman William Burke; militiaman Adolph Anderson credited with shooting Charles.

At least six named or distinct Black dead reported (Charles, the Jackson-house man, the Gallatin Street man, Thomas, Taylor, Mabry), plus three unidentified men killed July 25-26 who may include Thomas; no paper gives a full Black death count.
